newsitem.title: USA: Motorola says Ericsson comments not new.
newsitem.headline: Motorola says Ericsson comments not new.

text.p: Motorola Inc said Tuesday that comments by a competitor regarding continued pricing pressure in the telecommunications market are no different from the Schaumburg, Ill.-based company's own comments last month.
Earlier today, Telefon AB L.M. Ericsson of Sweden said it saw signs of continued pricing pressure on telecommunications products in 1997, similar to what it experienced in 1996.
"Ericsson's comments today are identical to the comment Motorola made when Motorola announced its fourth quarter results on January 9," Ed Gams, head of Motorola's investor relations said.
In a statement issued January 9, Motorola chief executive officer Christopher Galvin said the long-term outlook for the company's communications businesses remains promising.
"...(H)owever, many of the factors that affected certain of our businesses should continue to have an adverse impact in early 1997," Galvin said at the time.
A Motorola spokesman said Galvin was referring to pricing pressure in cellular and paging products.
Market sources said Ericsson's comments pressured Motorola's shares, which were off four at 63-1/2 in the early afternoon. Ericsson's shares were down four at 248 crowns.
Similarly, shares of Finnish telecommunications group Nokia Ab Oy were down 2.50 to 322 markka. Nokia declined to comment earlier today on Ericsson's statement about continued pricing pressure.
Motorola declined to comment on the drop in its stock price, citing company policy.
Motorola, a leading provider of wireless communications, semiconductors and electronics systems, said it has the number one market shares in paging and cellular phones worldwide.
While the actual market shares were not disclosed, Gams said Motorola has a "dominant number one position" in paging, with a market share that is more than twice that of its nearest competitor.
He added Motorola retains a "strong number one" position in cellular phones worldwide.
